# Applications for Baylor Applied Performance

## Where this applies

- Inference: Write a competition-demand profile per position group (football) and use it as the end point of a return-to-performance plan, the way the speaker builds basketball bout lengths, transition counts and speed ranges into rehab sessions [20:58]. For football that means play counts, series length and high-speed efforts from Catapult game data.
- Inference: Log a daily cumulative lower-limb load for athletes returning from tibial or foot injuries, from a shank-mounted accelerometer if Baylor ever adopts one, and share the trend with Athletic Medicine before imaging reviews [11:17]. The speaker says these proxies are not super precise [10:15].
- Inference: Track left and right footstrike counts at several intensity bands for returning lower-limb athletes if a suitable sensor exists, and watch for change in pattern from baseline, as the speaker describes [19:57].
- Inference: Pre-agree load progressions (low, then moderate, then high intensity) with Athletic Medicine before the athlete reaches full practice, using criteria rather than dates [13:19].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supplies information to support Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine on return-to-performance decisions, a support role [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]. The talk agrees with that framing (technology as a way to explain the plan to coaches and front office [23:02]) and says diagnosis must be right first [06:37].
- Eric's baseline: no specific return-to-play criteria or phased protocol appears in the corpus, and the section is the thinnest in the baseline [method-baseline.md Rehab and return to play]. The talk extends it: it offers a process (criterion-based progressions, demand profile) but no thresholds Baylor could copy.
- Eric's baseline: wellness-style subjective monitoring is kept for return-to-play where it adds context, and NordBord is kept for small targeted return-to-play groups [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md; 2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]. The talk agrees that clinical signs (swelling, stiffness, pain) still tune the model [10:45].
- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost versus insight and consistency matters more than test validity [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]. The talk agrees on caution: the wearable market is unregulated and unreliable data can mislead [04:05].
- Eric's baseline: smooth, gradual progression is treated as injury-risk control [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]. The talk agrees [07:08].

## What would have to be true

- A sensor with published or in-house validation for the specific use, since the speaker says the market is unregulated [04:05].
- A real baseline of the athlete's game and practice demands in the same sport, not another sport's numbers. The basketball figures do not transfer to football.
- Agreement from Athletic Medicine on who owns the decision. The talk puts the physical therapist and the strength coach in a handoff [12:19], which at Baylor is a departmental question.
- Athlete buy-in. The speaker says athletes accept the technology when it gives insight and resist it when it feels like policing [05:06].

## Do not apply when

- The diagnosis is uncertain. The speaker says no wearable saves a missed diagnosis [06:37].
- The sensor metric is treated as measured bone strain. The speaker calls it a surrogate proxy [09:42], and the evidence cited is rodent bone work [08:38] plus unspecified human studies, not a validated return-to-play rule.
- The league context differs: the NBA data are professional, one sport, and the talk's numbers (36 minutes per game, speeds of 6 to 17 mph [16:24] [17:25]) say nothing about college football.
- A single high-profile case drives the choice: the talk has no sample, no outcomes and no reinjury rates for the process.
- Data from the technology could reach the front office in ways that hurt athletes. The speaker names trust as a condition [22:01].

## First step

Draft a one-page "demands of competition" profile for one football position group from existing Catapult game data (series length, play counts, top-speed efforts) and hand it to Athletic Medicine as a possible end point for a return-to-practice progression. No new equipment needed.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: JuUBObeNGfc
title: "SSAC18: Using Lab Science and Field Analytics to Maximize Performance"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Aaron Bagga (caption spelling; host introduces him as "Dr." and a clinical cardiologist), Sam Feder (host)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, competitive-advantage, other-sport:rowing]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].
- Oxygen flows lung to heart and circulation to muscle, and all three links are trainable (the speaker hints lungs are not the one that changed here) [09:10].
- Heart rate, oxygen uptake and work rate are linear in a healthy person, while carbon dioxide output steepens above a point called the ventilatory threshold [10:10].
- That threshold is, in his view, the single most important measurement for elite athletes, and physiologically there are only two zones, below it (sustainable for hours with fuel and fluids) and above it (effort-dependent fatigue) [10:40] [11:10].
- Equations for max heart rate are unreliable and should be replaced by measurement [11:40].
- Easy days must sit clearly below the threshold and hard days clearly above it, with little to gain in between [17:17] [17:47].
- Coaches who apply physiology tend to win and those who ignore it lose, in his experience [18:48].
- A reassessment cycle in the lab, about every four months in this case, keeps the plan honest [19:19].
- Heart rate variability is a fickle measure and he has not seen it work alone at the elite level, though he accepts it as a backup to subjective recovery [22:54].
- Changes in the power-to-heart-rate relationship are the best sign of fitness change for athletes with power meters [25:26].
- The lab fits endurance-heavy athletes best, because anaerobic lab tests such as the Wingate engage different machinery from the sport [26:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Max heart rate prediction error: the true standard deviation is on the order of 15 to 20 beats per minute [12:11].
- Case athlete at baseline: measured max heart rate 208, peak oxygen uptake 71 mL per kg, threshold at 78% of max oxygen uptake at a heart rate of about 162 [12:41].
- Tracking period requested before any change: 90 days [13:11].
- Training before intervention: 13 sessions per week, about 18 hours, 11 base-building and 2 higher-intensity [13:41].
- Field heart rate: base sessions about 160 plus or minus 2, hard sessions about 12 beats higher, resting about 52, felt recovered 50% of the time [14:12]. Caption at [15:14] gives 180 and 172 for these sessions, which conflicts with 160 and +12; probably garbled.
- Doldrums: roughly 5 beats above and 5 below the threshold heart rate [16:46].
- Goal horizon: an 18-month periodized plan toward an Olympic team [18:18].
- Reassessment every four months, and the third reassessment came roughly eleven months later [19:19].
- After the program: threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise), peak heart rate unchanged, peak oxygen uptake only slightly higher [19:49].
- Field after: base heart rates in the 150s, hard intervals close to 180, resting heart rate lower [20:20]; felt recovered 70% of the time, up from 50% [20:51].
- Hard-interval average 179 with a standard deviation of 8 to 10 beats (caption wording unclear about which) [24:40].
- Subjective measure: a 1 to 10 satisfaction score for each workout [13:41].
- Context: program started in 2007 [05:05]; only one quarter of the studied masters athletes were risk-factor free [03:35].

## Methods and frameworks named

- A four-step sequence for suboptimal performance: medical evaluation, physiology evaluation, training evaluation, then planning, reassessment and implementation [07:07].
- Lab measures: max heart rate, aerobic efficiency (slope of oxygen against work), ventilatory threshold [12:11].
- Field data: 90 days of untouched training with a heart-rate monitor and a satisfaction rating [13:41].
- Training plan: individualize physiology, set a calendar working back from the goal event, assess the support structure (coach, nutrition, family), and run a longitudinal reassessment loop [16:46] [18:18].
- Sub-doldrum sessions are aerobic base, technique and active recovery. Supra-doldrum sessions include steady state, short and long intervals [17:17] [17:47].

## Limits and open questions

- One athlete, no control and no group data. Other changes during the eleven months are not shown.
- The speaker states his program has financial relationships with local and national groups (disclosed at [01:02]).
- Some figures are hard to verify due to captions (see Numbers).
- The oxygen-uptake threshold is described as "the single most important measurement" without data beyond the case.
- Heart rate variability skepticism is opinion, no data shown.
- Whether the same split works in team sports is not shown; he says the lab suits endurance components [26:27].

## Q&A

- Heart rate variability: promising in theory, many confounders, useful only as a backup to how the athlete feels [22:23] [22:54].
- Did the volume drop explain the gain: no, the key change was two clearly different kinds of days [23:33].
- Race-day intensity and the variance in hard sessions: hard sessions varied in effort to mimic race conditions, and he says most athletes improve when forced to rest after injury [24:10] [24:40].
- Power meters: pair power with heart rate, a rise in power at a given heart rate signals adaptation [25:26].
- Anaerobic power testing: Wingate is limited, better to use the sport's own exercises as benchmarks [25:56] [26:27].

## Summary

A university football performance staff member uses Catapult data, sliced play by play in OpenField, to compare what offensive linemen do in games with what they do in practice. He argues that total player load looks alike for linemen and wide receivers, but the make-up differs: linemen have contacts, short work bouts and little high-speed running. Practice contact load was far below game level, which he says risked detraining and a spike on Saturday. The talk also covers how he gained coach buy-in, a sprint-speed myth, and a practice-schedule change moving intensity to Friday. The evidence is one team and one season, with no controlled outcome.

## Key claims

- Coaches rely on subjective grading, and objective data reduce opinion-versus-opinion conflict [01:02] [01:32].
- Training should start from game demands and work backwards [02:02].
- A published group study reported what linemen cover in a game, but the speaker argues it reports load, not the actual demands [03:04].
- Linemen and wide receivers have similar total player load, but very different composition (explosive yardage, high-speed distance, max speed) [03:34].
- A line coach ignored his report until the data were reframed in terms the coach cared about [04:04] [04:34].
- A gyroscope-based line metric detects when a lineman drops into a stance, then counts contacts and load per contact [05:38].
- Runs bring more contact and passes bring more force absorption [07:13].
- Practice was far below game intensity in contact load, even on the most intense practice day [08:16] [08:47].
- Energy-system detraining may occur if the alactic system is only stimulated on game day [08:47].
- Even contact periods in practice (first-team offense versus first-team defense, scout team) gave few game-like reps [09:18] [09:48].
- Speed is overrated for football: very few plays reach 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Intensity should rise while volume holds, because raising both creates fatigue [15:35].
- Moving the fast session to Friday (instead of a walkthrough) raised subjective and objective readiness on game day in his program [16:05] [16:36].
- Athletes must be shown their own data to get buy-in, or they feel like "lab rats" [17:38].
- A compromise with receivers: trim low-value periods and ask for full speed in the remaining ones, with load unchanged [18:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- Lineman game distance from the cited study: about 3,600 yards [01:32].
- Player load: summed movement from the unit, described as a more elaborate step counter [03:34].
- Average play duration: about 8 seconds, 7 for a run and 8 for a pass [06:10].
- Time between plays: about 30 seconds for his team, not up-tempo; some teams aim for under 18 seconds [06:42].
- Average load per contact: about 2.12 for pass, 2.32 for run, 2.22 combined [06:42] [07:13] [07:45].
- Contacts per game for a lineman: about 45 [07:13].
- Most intense practice: load per contact 1.54 against 2.22 in games [08:47].
- Alactic stimulus guideline: lose it if not stimulated every five to eight days [08:47].
- Game-like reps in practice: about 3.5 in one period and 1.5 in another, around five total [09:48].
- Contacts as a share of game player load: caption says "a hundred sixty-six percent" and then "sixty six percent", so likely 66% (caption garbled) [10:19].
- Contact load rises by over 100% from practice to game [10:19].
- Work-to-rest ratio about 1 to 3.75 [10:50].
- Fewer than 1% of more than 1,000 plays reached 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Average lineman travel per play: 13.5 yards, with direction split about 25% left and 25% right [11:52].
- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance in practice [13:27].
- Three-hour camp practice example: about 7,000 yards for a skill player, pacing at 17 to 18 mph [15:05].
- Eight-second work bouts fall under ten seconds all-out, treated as alactic [10:50].

## Methods and frameworks named

- OpenField used to slice each play in the game files [04:04].
- Offensive-line metric from the gyroscope: stance detection, contacts, load per contact, percent contact load [05:38].
- Practice versus game comparison by period type (individual, seven on seven, team versus scout) [09:18].
- Bioenergetic profile (work, rest) plus a movement profile to define what a lineman needs [12:22].
- Tapered week with a Friday fast session, tracked with wellness questionnaires and heart rate variability from a wearable [16:05].

## Limits and open questions

- One program and one season, no sample size given for contacts or practice periods.
- No evidence that closing the gap changes performance or injury. A question on this was asked and answered with his current approach, not outcomes [14:35] [15:05].
- Adding contact is limited by concussion risk, and the speaker had not yet solved this [12:22] [12:52].
- Heart rate variability is described as mixed: good and bad signals [16:05].
- The "Fast Friday" result is his team's own change, no controls.
- The speaker presents on behalf of Kentucky and the sponsor Catapult, who supply the units, and the caption suggests a company-sponsored session.
- Garbled captions: contacts-share percentage, and some wording in [05:06] and [10:50].

## Q&A

- Evidence that raising practice intensity helps game performance or fatigue: keep load constant and raise intensity, shorter sharper practices, and the Friday change [14:35] [15:05].
- Heart rate variability and wellness use: used, mixed results, Friday intensity improved readiness [16:05] [16:36].
- Player pushback (the Eagles with Chip Kelly were cited as an earlier case): show athletes their data and trim wasted periods so intensity is high in the remaining ones [17:38] [18:08].
- Contact: the speaker invites email and Twitter follow-up [18:38].

## Summary

A 76ers performance-research director argues that wearables can improve return-to-play by adding two things: a surrogate for the load an injured limb actually receives, and a profile of what a game will demand. He says the process matters more than the product. He links rehab load to tissue-loading research, uses shin-mounted accelerometers as a rough bone-load proxy, and uses game tracking and publicly available data to define the bursts and transitions an athlete must be ready for. He also says trust matters: athletes accept devices that give insight and reject ones that feel like policing. No outcome data are shown, so it is a conceptual framework.

## Key claims

- Return to play is a negotiation between agents (reinjury risk), front office and coaches (missed games), and the athlete [02:02] [02:33].
- Wearables fall into two types, what the athlete does and how the body responds, and both together are most informative [03:34].
- The market is unregulated, so data reliability must be checked or artifacts can mislead [04:05] [04:35].
- Devices used to police athletes get pushed back, while devices that provide insight are welcomed [05:06].
- Injury databases are contaminated because some absences are strategic, but are accurate enough for trends [06:06].
- Accurate diagnosis comes first, and no wearable fixes a misdiagnosis [06:37].
- Rehab should follow criterion-based progressions grounded in how tendons, ligaments and bone respond to load [07:08].
- Practice style can differ from game style, so a player who scrimmaged may still face an unaccustomed high-intensity exposure [07:38].
- Tissue has a loading sweet spot: too much stress stalls or breaks down, too little gives no collagen resynthesis [08:08] [08:38].
- A tibia-mounted accelerometer can give a rough low, moderate or severe bone-load proxy and a daily cumulative load, to be read alongside clinical signs [10:15] [10:45].
- If imaging shows poor response, loads can be stepped back to a previously tolerated level [11:48].
- Sensors can show ground-contact loading and left-right symmetry during water running and anti-gravity treadmill work [12:19] [12:49].
- Game demands should be profiled before clearing a player, and the fundamentals of basketball running distance were measured as early as 1931 [15:22] [15:53].
- Matching skill actions (catches, passes, shots, defensive slides, contacts) gives the athlete confidence and a way to communicate readiness to owners, general managers and coaches [20:27].
- Athletes in rehab welcome devices that help them build a bridge back, but are suspicious if data could leak into trades or sales [21:29] [22:01].

## Numbers and definitions

- About 1 in 4 NBA athletes will have an ankle injury that costs at least one game [05:36].
- A progression of six to eight weeks of monitored load, with no pain, swelling or stiffness, before the athlete returns to full practice [13:49].
- Loading range from under one times body weight to about seven and a half or eight times body weight per footstrike [13:19].
- 1931 study: a guard ran about two to two and a half miles, against public guesses of 5 to 10 [15:53]; running bursts of about two minutes at three to four miles per hour [15:53].
- 2016-17: a high-minute player averaged about 36 minutes, the 1931 player about 40, covering similar distance and speeds [16:24] [16:54].
- Tracking data: 1.2 to 1.5 million data points, mostly 6 to 10 mph, with some runs at 13 to 14 and up to 17 mph [17:25].
- Running bursts of 90 to 120 seconds are common, often under 30 seconds, sometimes three minutes without a break (the captions say three to four minutes) [17:55].
- Rehab profile targets: segments of three to six minutes, transitions every ten to twenty seconds, continuous play up to three minutes, six to eight full-court transitions [20:58].
- Caption trouble: company names, co-author first names and the cited bone study author are garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- A pathway: diagnosis, medical treatment, load-based rehab, demand-matched practice, game return [06:37] [07:08] [07:38].
- Mechanobiological approach: link sensor-derived load to tissue-loading research (rodent bone and ligament work cited) [09:42].
- Shank-mounted accelerometers, waterproofed sensors for pool and anti-gravity work, and RFID-style player tracking for games [10:15] [12:49] [14:20].
- Publicly available tracking data used to build speed distribution, burst length and recovery profiles [17:25] [17:55].
- Symmetry patterns by intensity band from a New Zealand pro team across a season [19:26].

## Limits and open questions

- No return-to-play outcomes, reinjury rates or sample sizes are shown. Bone proxies are described as not super precise [10:15].
- Load-response evidence cited is largely rodent and laboratory work [08:38].
- The speaker discloses his team's involvement with two companies and says no one receives money from them [01:02] [01:32]. One device was approved by the league's wearables committee and another was in process [01:02].
- No numeric thresholds for clearance are given.
- The speaker acknowledges practice-versus-game mismatch but gives no matching rule beyond the demand profiles.
- Captions garble names (the two companies, the study author), so these should not be relied on.

## Q&A

No Q&A in the transcript.

Video 2 [10:19] "hundred sixty-six percent"/"sixty six percent" garbled; some sentences in [05:06] unclear. Video 3 company names, "BER" study author, and co-author names garbled; "Messersmith" and "DePauw" are caption spellings; I did not verify any claim against outside sources.
